Chinese President Xi Jinping meets with Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, November 19, 2026. /Xinhua
Chinese President Xi Jinping met with Russian President Vladimir Putin and US President Donald Trump on Thursday in the southern Chinese city of Shenzhen, in an unprecedented gathering with far-reaching implications for the world.
At a time of growing geopolitical uncertainty and intensifying competition among major powers, experts said the trilateral engagement could help manage differences, reduce the risk of confrontation and create opportunities for cooperation in areas ranging from energy and food security to artificial intelligence (AI).
More importantly, experts said, it points to a possible new approach to major-power relations – one that recognizes differences while maintaining dialogue and pursuing shared interests. But they also stressed that lasting stability will depend on whether political dialogue can translate into reliable communication mechanisms, effective crisis management and tangible cooperation.
Dialogue and crisis management underpin global stability
During Thursday's meeting, President Xi said humanity lives in the same global village, where major countries shoulder special responsibilities. Their positive interaction, he stressed, is not optional but a necessity.
The Chinese president also outlined four principles for major powers to get along and jointly uphold world peace: mutual respect, peaceful coexistence, win-win cooperation and dialogue and consultation.
Zhang Tengjun, an associate research fellow at the Institute of American Studies at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences, told CGTN that relations among China, Russia and the United States have a direct bearing on global strategic stability and the future direction of the international order, given their positions as major powers and permanent members of the UN Security Council.
He said that the meeting establishes a direct channel for communication at the highest level and that its significance lies not in dividing the world into spheres of influence or establishing a system of trilateral governance, but in managing differences, reducing the risk of strategic miscalculation and preventing major-power relations from descending into confrontation or even a new Cold War.
Sun Taiyi, an associate professor of political science at Christopher Newport University in the United States, said that the meeting is historically significant because it creates an opportunity for the three countries to discuss their shared responsibility for strategic stability despite their differences.
"All three countries have an interest in preventing catastrophic conflict," Sun said, adding that constructive trilateral engagement could help counter bloc confrontation and demonstrate that cooperation between countries does not necessarily require exclusive alliances directed against others.
However, Sun cautioned that a single meeting cannot resolve the structural differences among the three powers. Lasting stability requires institutional mechanisms capable of withstanding disagreements and disputes.
He suggested prioritizing reliable crisis hotlines and AI-enabled emergency communication channels to clarify military intentions, share information on incidents and prevent miscalculations. Such mechanisms could also help governments quickly distinguish AI-related system malfunctions or false military warnings from deliberate attacks, reducing the risk of unintended escalation.
Safeguarding the post-war international order
Beyond managing immediate geopolitical risks, the meeting also carries implications for preserving the international order established after World War II.
During the talks, Xi stressed that China, Russia and the United States, as the main victors of World War II, should safeguard the postwar international order, uphold the purposes and principles of the UN Charter and defend the hard-won outcomes of victory in World War II.
Zhang said the three countries' dialogue provides an opportunity to reaffirm their shared historical responsibilities, oppose attempts to distort the history of World War II and defend the international system centered on the United Nations and the international order based on international law.
Such a commitment could help build consensus through multilateral platforms, resist unilateralism and the logic of power politics and reinforce the authority and role of the UN Security Council, he said.
Sun emphasized that safeguarding the post-war order also means strengthening the United Nations and respecting the rights of smaller countries.
"Major powers can help reduce confrontation and create openings for diplomacy, but they cannot confer legitimacy on arrangements simply by agreeing among themselves," he said.
For China, the trilateral dialogue offers an opportunity to demonstrate that a rising power can support the existing multilateral institutional framework while advocating reforms that give developing countries a greater voice in global governance, Sun added.
Turning political understanding into practical cooperation
Despite differences among the three countries, experts believe their shared interests in several areas could provide a foundation for future practical cooperation.
Zhang identified food and energy security, nuclear risk reduction, global governance and regional crisis management as potential priorities.
On food and energy, the three countries could work to maintain stable global supply chains, reduce trade barriers and unilateral export restrictions imposed in the name of national security and coordinate policies to curb excessive market volatility.
On nuclear issues, regular consultations on strategic forces, arms control and non-proliferation could help reduce the risks of miscalculation and unintended conflict.
He also called for greater coordination within the UN framework on climate change, public health and global poverty reduction, alongside regular high-level communication to promote political solutions to regional conflicts.
Sun identified energy and food security, nuclear risk reduction and AI safety as particularly promising areas for cooperation.
The three countries could explore arrangements to protect commercial shipping, minimize disruptions to civilian energy infrastructure and facilitate grain and fertilizer deliveries, he said. Such efforts should involve relevant coastal states, producers and importing countries, with UN agencies helping coordinate implementation.
On nuclear issues, US-Russia arms-reduction discussions could proceed alongside a broader trilateral dialogue on risk reduction, with China initially participating as an observer in selected discussions, Sun suggested.
AI safety could be addressed through a separate cooperation track involving emergency contacts, incident reporting and joint research into potentially dangerous AI capabilities.
But turning political understanding into tangible results will require more than broad commitments.
"The key is to give each issue an implementation process," Sun said, suggesting designated officials, clear timelines for follow-up meetings and measurable outcomes.
He said that delivering tangible benefits, even on a limited scale, would help build confidence and give strategic stability a practical foundation beyond the summit itself.

Editor's note: As AI makes cyberattacks cheaper, faster and more scalable, ordinary users face growing risks – from personalized scams to hijacked AI agents. Who will protect them? Duan Haixin, a professor at the Institute for Network Sciences and Cyberspace, Tsinghua University, examines how China, the EU and the US are tackling the challenge, and why personal vigilance alone is not enough. The article reflects the author's opinions, and not necessarily those of CGTN.
In April, American AI firm Anthropic launched Project Glasswing. It gave about 50 technology firms and open-source organizations, including Microsoft, Cisco, Amazon, Apple, NVIDIA and the Linux Foundation, access to Claude Mythos Preview, an unreleased frontier model, to hunt for previously unknown "zero-day" flaws. Mozilla's Firefox team used it to find and fix 271 vulnerabilities, 180 of them rated high severity.
Three months later, the tables turned. During an internal security test at OpenAI, a group of AI agents exploited a software flaw to escape their testing sandbox. They broke into Hugging Face, a major platform for AI developers, and gained administrator access to its server cluster. OpenAI said the agents inferred the platform might hold material related to the test, and its later investigation identified cheating on the evaluation as a key factor.
AI-driven vulnerability hunting helps defenders find weaknesses early. But attackers can use the same tools to find flaws and strike, leaving defenders far less time to patch and ordinary users facing greater risk.
How AI magnifies the threat to ordinary users
AI changes cyberattacks in speed, scale and cost. For ordinary users the drop in cost matters most. Researching an individual, crafting a convincing story and keeping up a conversation used to take real human effort. AI has made all of this cheap, so personalized scams can now be run at scale. This shows up in three ways.
1. Fraud is moving from generic mass messages to personalized ones produced in bulk. Impersonating relatives, posing as customer service and sending phishing links are old tricks. Now AI can write scripts tailored to a target's identity, background and needs, backed by cloned voices and deepfake video. Faked faces may also get past weak identity checks.
2. The answers AI gives can be manipulated for profit. This year, China Media Group's annual March 15 consumer rights gala exposed an "AI poisoning" industry that fabricates reviews and rankings to shape what AI models recommend. The more people rely on AI for shopping advice, the more they should ask where an answer comes from and who benefits, instead of treating it as objective fact.
3. AI agents that act on users' behalf are becoming targets themselves. Once an AI agent can read your emails, open your files or operate your accounts, an attacker can hide instructions in an email, web page or document that turn it against you, getting it to leak data or take actions you never approved. Such "indirect prompt injection" attacks have already been reported in consumer office software. The more access an agent has, the more damage it can do once hijacked.
Different approaches, a shared challenge
China pairs development with security and sets rules by sector and use. Its interim measures on generative AI require services with public-opinion attributes or the capacity for social mobilization to undergo security assessments and algorithm filing, and to deal with and report illegal content promptly. The AI Safety Governance Framework 3.0, released in September, updates risk categories and countermeasures and adds dedicated provisions on AI agent risks.
The European Union's AI Act sets obligations according to risk. Providers of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk must carry out adversarial testing, assess and mitigate systemic risks, protect their models' cybersecurity and report serious incidents. Violations stemming from intent or negligence trigger fines of up to 3% of global annual turnover or 15 million euros, whichever is higher.
The United States leans toward innovation and voluntary cooperation. A June executive order sets up a voluntary framework under which developers may give the federal government up to 30 days of access to certain frontier models before sharing them with other trusted partners. The order states that this creates no mandatory licensing or pre-approval requirement. Whether such voluntary arrangements will work remains to be seen.
Different as these paths may be, they share one challenge. Principles have to be turned into security measures that cover an AI system's whole life cycle and can be continuously verified. The model is only one component of the system. Software components, data services, credentials, tool interfaces and runtime environments matter just as much, and the incidents above show how flaws in them let attackers or rogue agents to bypass isolation, escalate privileges and reach external systems. Treating "model compliance" as equivalent to "system security" leaves these risks unaddressed.
What individuals can do, and where policy must step in
With AI making attackers more efficient, ordinary users need to get the basics right. Keep systems updated, use different passwords for important accounts and turn on two-step verification. Install software and AI services only from official sources, and keep an offline backup of important files. Verify any request for money or identity checks through a number you saved yourself or an official channel, never by voice or video alone. Give AI agents only the permissions a task requires.
Personal vigilance, however, cannot replace corporate responsibility and public oversight. Responsibility should follow the ability to control risk. AI companies should keep assessing risks and improving safeguards. Product makers should patch vulnerabilities promptly. Companies that suffer a data leak should handle it strictly by the book and notify affected users immediately. AI systems capable of operating external devices and accounts should run under strict, least-privilege principles, keep immutable logs and require human confirmation for high-risk actions like financial transactions. Policy must also expand security scope to cover the entire underlying software stack, while legally protecting security researchers who disclose flaws lawfully, ensuring bureucratic hurdles never weaken our collective defense.
The good news is that AI is also making defense cheaper, as the Firefox case shows. China's Framework 3.0 calls for making AI security capabilities widely accessible. Policy should make sure these capabilities reach small organizations and ordinary users, so that technological progress narrows the security gap rather than widening it.

Zhai Jun, special envoy of the Chinese government on the Middle East issue, Liu Xianfa, special representative of the Chinese government on African affairs, and Hu Changchun, special envoy for the Horn of Africa Affairs of the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, recently visited seven countries across the Middle East, the Gulf, the Red Sea and the Horn of Africa, engaging with regional parties and calling for dialogue and peace.
In an exclusive interview with China Media Group (CMG) after their visits, the three envoys outlined China's diplomatic efforts, the challenges to achieving a lasting ceasefire and the country's proposals for regional peace and stability.
Zhai Jun, special envoy of the Chinese government on the Middle East issue, speaks to CMG. /CMG
Supporting regional countries in resolving disputes through dialogue
Since September, clashes involving Yemen's Houthi group, Saudi Arabia and Yemeni government forces have intensified, while security risks in the Red Sea have also increased. Conflicts across the Middle East remain interconnected, raising concerns over further regional spillover.
During his recent visits to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia, Chinese envoy Zhai met with officials from the three countries and discussed the situation in Yemen with relevant parties, explaining China's positions and proposals.
Zhai said China believes that the use of force cannot resolve disputes and that escalating regional instability serves no one's interests. He called on all parties to exercise restraint, avoid further tensions and seek solutions through diplomatic channels.
Zhai said China's diplomatic engagements had reinforced the sense that peace, development and the ability to determine their own future are shared aspirations among people in the Middle East.
He outlined China's approach to mediating regional issues, including supporting Middle Eastern countries in pursuing strategic autonomy, unity and self-reliance, while opposing external interference. China also encourages regional countries to resolve disputes through dialogue and consultation based on the merits of each issue, he said.
China has put forward a series of proposals since April, including a four-point proposal on promoting peace and stability in the Middle East, the four principles for resolving the Palestinian question, and a four-point proposal on a new security architecture for the Middle East.
Zhai stressed that lasting stability requires common security among regional countries. He called on the international community to address the Palestinian question, which he described as a root cause of instability in the Middle East, and take into account the links between regional conflicts.
He also urged joint efforts to safeguard the security of key shipping routes, energy supplies and industrial and supply chains, adding that China would continue to play a constructive role in promoting peace and stability in the region.
Liu Xianfa, special representative of the Chinese government on African affairs, speaks to CMG. /CMG
Horn of Africa must not become a geopolitical battleground
While Zhai was visiting the Gulf region, Liu visited Ethiopia, Djibouti and Egypt, and Hu traveled to Eritrea. They called on regional countries to strengthen cooperation, safeguard peace and pursue development.
The Red Sea connects the Atlantic Ocean, the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean, serving as a major maritime corridor linking Asia, Africa and Europe. It carries around 12% of global maritime trade and 30% of container traffic.
With disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz amid the prolonged conflict, the Red Sea has become increasingly important. Rising tensions there pose serious risks to trade, investment, energy and food security in the Horn of Africa.
Liu said China had proposed the Outlook on Peace and Development in the Horn of Africa to support regional countries in addressing security, development and governance challenges independently and collectively.
Hu Changchun, special envoy for the Horn of Africa Affairs of the Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs, speaks to CMG. /CMG
Hu said security challenges remain the biggest obstacle to development and revitalization in the Horn of Africa and across the continent. He stressed the importance of strategic autonomy, Pan-Africanism and greater unity among African countries.
China's strong political trust and practical cooperation with its 53 African diplomatic partners provide a solid foundation for its constructive participation in addressing regional issues, Hu said.
China also supports regional development by helping countries address development gaps and reduce the conditions that fuel conflict. Chinese peacekeepers in missions in Darfur, Sudan and South Sudan have also contributed to maintaining peace and stability, he added.
Liu acknowledged that significant challenges remain to achieving lasting peace in the Horn of Africa. He said some external countries had pursued geopolitical interests by creating divisions, fueling confrontation and using regional issues as political tools, undermining efforts to resolve conflicts.
China is ready to work with all countries and people committed to peace and development to implement the Global Security Initiative and contribute to Africa's prosperity and long-term stability, Liu said.

Nvidia has reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as president and chief executive officer, reversing its earlier position on his departure. The company's board of directors voted unanimously to restore Huang to the positions, effective immediately, and reinstate him as a board member, the company announced on November 23.
The decision followed a series of discussions between Huang and the board, which said it was satisfied with his candor and leadership capabilities. The board also consulted senior US government officials and concluded that Huang's return would pose no national security risk.
Jensen Huang gives a keynote address at the Nvidia Berlin GPU Technology Conference in Berlin, Germany, October 21, 2026. 
Board Chair Harvey C. Jones said Huang was the right person to lead Nvidia and that his reinstatement was in the best interests of the company's shareholders, employees, partners and customers. Jones will remain board chair. Colette Kress, who served as interim CEO during Huang's absence, will continue in her role as chief financial officer.
Huang voluntarily resigned on November 12 after the board raised concerns about his personal conduct, which it said was inconsistent with the company's code of conduct, standards and corporate culture. At Nvidia's quarterly earnings call on November 17, Jones said the board had unanimously accepted the resignation and did not intend to reinstate Huang. Kress was appointed interim CEO, and the company began searching for a permanent successor.
The board's latest decision came after a wave of public support for Huang's return. Reuters reported that a petition calling for his reinstatement had attracted more than 180,000 signatures, including one from Tesla CEO Elon Musk. US President Donald Trump, who had urged Nvidia to bring Huang back the previous week, welcomed the board's decision on Monday, calling it the "correct and proper decision" in a post on Truth Social. Trump also said the US government had no reason to believe Huang's return posed a national security risk and urged Nvidia to continue ensuring compliance with US export controls.
Despite Huang's return, an independent investigation launched by the board will continue. Nvidia said the committee overseeing the inquiry, composed entirely of independent directors and supported by outside legal counsel, would carry its investigation through to completion. Huang has pledged full cooperation.
The company has also established a separate National Security and Export Control Committee, made up exclusively of independent directors, to oversee trade compliance and national security risks. The committee is engaging legal counsel with relevant expertise, while Nvidia is seeking to appoint a chief compliance officer to oversee compliance across the company and report to the board's Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee.
